title: An API for Kotlin and Java callers
goal: By the end you can put a subscription DSL on top of the bus with `@DslMarker` and reified inline helpers, give Java callers a surface that reads like ordinary Java (`Class<T>` overloads, `@JvmOverloads`, `@JvmStatic`, a facade over the value classes) that still validates, and defend each generics and patterns choice in the library to a sceptical reviewer.
opening:
Pedal Post's depot has two doors. Riders who work there every day come in at the front and speak the house shorthand: "PP-7781, collected, two and a half." Drivers from a partner courier use the side door, where a clerk hands them the standard printed form. Both doors lead to the same sorting room, under the same rules.

Our library needs both doors. The Kotlin team wants to wire a dozen handlers in a few lines it can read at a glance. The support team writes Java, and Java sees our Kotlin only through the compiled class files, where a reified function vanishes and a getter is called `getWeight-RqKWbHU`. The easy trap is to build the side door by loosening the rules, so that Java can pass in raw numbers nobody checks.

A typed event bus gave us delivery. In this last sitting of Part 3, we'll write a small subscription language for Kotlin and keep its nested blocks in their place. Then we'll give Java a door that still checks everything, and finish with a design review. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A Java class needs a handler for `ParcelCollected`. The Kotlin bus offers `fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>)` and `inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>)`. What can the Java team write?
options: `bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, h)`
`bus.<ParcelCollected>subscribe(h)`
`bus.subscribe(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(ParcelCollected.class), h)`
Nothing: Java can't call either function
warmup.why: A `Class` is not a `KClass`, so the first call doesn't match, however natural it looks. The reified function is compiled as a synthetic method, and javac ignores synthetic methods, so the second finds nothing. The `KClass` version works once Java converts the class by hand, which reads badly. This lesson adds a `Class<E>` overload so Java can write the first line.

sections.h: What Java sees, and a side door that still checks everything
sections.body:
javac, the Java compiler, never reads our Kotlin source. It reads the class files kotlinc wrote, and it reads them very literally. Here is what it finds when Java code meets the API as Kotlin developers usually write it. Every error below comes from the demo:

| Kotlin as written | What Java gets | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| `inline fun <reified E> subscribe(h)` | invisible: `no suitable method found for subscribe((e)->{ })` | a `Class<E>` overload |
| `fun <E> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, h)` | callable through `JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class)` | the same overload |
| a constructor with default arguments | `new PlainBus()` and the full one only: `no suitable constructor found for PlainBus(String)` | `@JvmOverloads` |
| a member of an `object` | `Registry.INSTANCE.publish(...)` | `@JvmStatic` |
| a companion `val SYSTEM` | `Ticker.Companion.getSYSTEM()` | `@JvmField` |
| top-level functions in `Timing.kt` | `TimingKt.timed(...)` | `@file:JvmName("Handlers")` |
| a data class with value-class properties | `ParcelCollected(String,long) has private access in ParcelCollected`, getters such as `getWeight-RqKWbHU()` | a facade |

Read the table one row at a time with the earlier tracks in mind. A reified function is the clerk's note, and javac can't write one: it can't paste Kotlin code into a Java caller, so kotlinc marks the function synthetic, made by the compiler and hidden from Java source. Type erasure and reified type parameters gave the answer: Java hands over the class itself, `ParcelCollected.class`, so the bus needs an overload, a second `subscribe` with the same name that takes Java's `Class<E>`. The annotations each ask kotlinc for one small thing. `@JvmOverloads` asks for one Java constructor per default argument. `@JvmStatic` makes an `object`'s member a real static method. `@JvmField` exposes a constant as a plain field, and `@file:JvmName` names the class that holds a file's top-level functions.

The facade is the decision that matters, because it touches the checks. A facade, the hotel reception desk from Adapter and Facade, is one small object that gives outsiders a simple way in. Value classes and what they compile to warned that `@JvmName` on a function that takes a value class lets Java pass a raw `long` straight past `init`. Our facade does the opposite. It takes plain values and builds the value classes itself, so every `init` block runs:

```java
ParcelCollected c = Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500);    // validates: "7781" throws
long grams = Events.grams(c);
bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, e -> loadBoard.add(Events.parcelId(e), Events.grams(e)));
```

```kotlin
object Events {
    @JvmStatic
    fun collected(parcelId: String, grams: Long): ParcelCollected =
        ParcelCollected(ParcelId(parcelId), Weight(grams))          // the init blocks run

    @JvmStatic
    fun grams(event: Handover): Long = event.weight.grams
}
```

`@JvmExposeBoxed`, Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and switched on with an opt-in, would give Java `new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(...), new Weight(...))` and a boxed getter. In a quick test with its module-wide flag, the getter on the event interface itself stayed mangled, so Java code that knows only `ParcelEvent` would still need `Events.parcelId(e)`. Keep the facade until that changes.

Some of the Java surface came free from earlier decisions. Lesson 2's `Handler<in E>` shows up as `Handler<? super E>`, so a Java `Handler<ParcelEvent>` fits any subscription, and the lab's Java support desk counts failed deliveries with one. kotlinc writes `PermittedSubclasses` for the sealed model, so a Java `switch` over a `ParcelEvent` with one case per leaf compiles with no `default`. `Subscription.close()` declares no checked exception, the kind Java forces every caller to catch, so try-with-resources needs no `catch`. And because handlers and middleware are `fun interface`s with `void` and `int` methods, no Java lambda ever returns `Unit.INSTANCE`.

Uncomment the four lines at the end of `JavaViewDemo.java` one at a time, and predict javac's complaint before each run.

sections.h: Design review: defend each choice, or say when you'd undo it
sections.body:
A design review is a meeting where you explain each choice in a design while someone sceptical asks why. It's where you find out which decisions you can defend. Here are the questions I'd expect about this library, with the answer I'd give. Disagree where your program differs.

"Why value classes, if Java needs a facade?" Keep them. In the Kotlin model, a swapped id and weight don't compile, and an invalid tracking number can't exist. The facade costs one file. If most callers were Java, I'd undo it and use plain records with compact constructors.

"A `Weight` has no unit." Keep it. The one-field rule made that choice cheap, and the door is the right place for any other unit: a partner's pounds become grams in the parser, once. A unit field inside `Weight` would cost an object per weight and buy nothing.

"Supertype dispatch will surprise people." Keep it, and write it down. The sealed hierarchy keeps the set of keys small, fixed and testable, and the order is a tested promise. The surprise to warn about is the other side of that promise: a `ParcelEvent` handler also hears every event type added next year.

"`in`, adapters, casts: isn't that a lot of machinery?" Keep `in`: it's what lets one tracking handler serve every subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. The single cast is checked by `type.cast` and guaranteed by the keys.

"Delivery is synchronous and lives in memory." Keep it for connecting the parts of one program. Undo it for anything that must survive a crash or reach another program, because the bus forgets everything when the program stops. Those events need storage that survives a restart, such as a database table written in the same step as the change, or a message broker. Guava's documentation for its own `EventBus` lists no way to slow a fast publisher, little control over threads and no exception passing among its reasons to look elsewhere. This bus fixes the last one with an `ErrorHandler`, and not the first two.

"`DropDuplicates` remembers every event for ever." Undo it as written. Bound it to a window of recent events, or let the handler keep its own record of the scans it has seen, which also survives a restart.

"The DSL commits after the block. What if `commit` fails halfway?" Today `subscribe` can't fail. If it ever can, `commit` must close what it already opened before it rethrows.

Notice the pattern in the answers. A choice is safe when an earlier lesson's mechanism forces it: `in` for a consumer, no `else` on a sealed `when`, a `Class<E>` overload because Java can't call a reified function. It's a judgment call when it trades cost for safety: value classes with a facade, synchronous delivery, a memory with no limit. Those are the ones to write down, with the condition that would make you undo them.

try.title: Write your own review notes
steps: Without looking back, list five design choices in the library you built across the three labs.
For each, write one line: keep or undo, the earlier lesson whose mechanism decides it, and the condition that would change your answer.
Pick the choice you're least sure about and write the test that would tell you that you were wrong.
try.expect: A strong list mixes forced choices (no `else` on the sealed `when`, `Handler<in E>`, a `Class<E>` overload because Java can't call reified functions) with judgment calls (value classes plus a facade, synchronous delivery in memory, an unbounded `DropDuplicates`). The forced ones cite a mechanism. The judgment calls cite a condition, such as "undo when most callers are Java" or "undo when an event must survive a restart".

compare.title: The same wiring from Kotlin and from Java

java.title: LoadBoardWiring.java

kotlin.title: LoadBoardWiring.kt

compare.note: Both wire the same three subscriptions on the same bus, and both get one handle back. The Kotlin version reads the domain types directly (`it.parcelId`, `it.weight`) and uses `on<E>` with a reified type, inside a `timed` group whose handlers can't reach the outer builder by accident. The Java version passes `Class` tokens, gets plain `String` and `long` through the `Events` facade, and times handlers one by one with `Handlers.timed`, because a Kotlin receiver lambda would cost it a `return Unit.INSTANCE`. What doesn't differ is the safety: the same `init` blocks check events built from Java, `Handler<? super E>` lets the Java tracking handler fit any subscription, and javac can switch exhaustively over the Kotlin sealed model.

worked.title: Add subscribeOnce, with its Kotlin sugar and its Java door

steps.say: A welcome text must go out for a new sender's first collection only. Start with the core, in Kotlin, taking a `KClass`. The handle closes itself, and `compareAndSet` makes sure only one of eight publishing threads runs the handler, the balking idea from *Concurrency patterns that tie it all together*. One race needs care: an event can arrive before `handle.set` has run, so the code closes again after setting it.
steps.alt_code:
// What Java sees for the core: a KClass parameter it can only reach the long way round.
bus.subscribeOnce(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(ParcelCollected.class), c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Kotlin sugar: a one-line reified wrapper. It needs no `noinline` or `crossinline`: its parameter is a `Handler`, not a function type, so there is nothing to inline.
steps.alt_code:
// Java can't see the reified wrapper: javac reports "no suitable method found for subscribeOnce"
bus.subscribeOnce(c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Java door: a `Class<E>` overload that converts and delegates. Because `Handler` is declared `in`, Java sees `Handler<? super E>`, so a general handler fits too.
steps.code:
fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription =
    subscribeOnce(type.kotlin, handler)

steps.say: Last, pin it from both sides. A Kotlin test publishes the same collection from eight threads and checks that one text went out. A Java test makes the Java call above, so a Kotlin-side change that breaks Java callers fails in this module's own build.

lab.title: Put a DSL and a Java door on the bus
steps: The package starts with lesson 2's solution, already given its Java-facing annotations: `@JvmOverloads` on the bus constructor, `@JvmField` on `ErrorHandler.PRINT` and `Ticker.SYSTEM`, `@file:JvmName("Handlers")` on `Timing.kt`. Read them first. Don't edit `Callers.kt`. Run the tests: all thirteen fail, six Kotlin and seven Java.
`Bus.kt` TODO 1: the `Class<E>` overload of `subscribe`, in one line.

`Dsl.kt` TODO 2: add `@DslMarker` to `EventsDsl`, and `@EventsDsl` to both builder classes. TODO 3: `on` adds a `Pending`; `commit` sets `committed`, subscribes every entry and returns one handle that closes them in reverse.
TODO 4: the reified `on<E>`. Write `on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) })`, compile, and add the modifier the error asks for. TODO 5: `TimedGroup`'s two `on` functions.
`JavaApi.kt` TODO 6: `collected`, `parcelId`, `grams` and the `Consumer` entry point.
`SupportDesk.java` TODO 7: one `Events.subscriptions` block with two `b.on(...)` calls.
Run until all thirteen pass. Then delete `@JvmStatic` from `Events.collected` and run once more: read what javac says about `FromJavaTest`, and put it back.
hints: `Events.subscriptions` is `SubscriptionsBuilder.build(bus, timings) { block.accept(this) }`: inside the receiver lambda, `this` is the builder.
In `SupportDesk`, `failedAttempts.merge(Events.parcelId(event), 1, Integer::sum)` adds one to the parcel's running count, and `deliveredGrams.addAndGet(Events.grams(d))` adds a delivery's weight.
The `Handler<ParcelEvent>` for failed deliveries compiles in `b.on(DeliveryFailed.class, ...)` because Java sees `Handler<? super E>`.
lab.done_when: All thirteen tests in `DslTest` and `FromJavaTest` pass.

drill.title: The DSL skeleton and the Java door from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write the Kotlin entry function `subscriptions`, the builder's `on(type, handler)`, `commit()` and the reified `on<E>` (with the right modifier). Then, below it, write the Java call that wires one delivery handler through `Events.subscriptions`, and name the annotation or overload behind each part of that Java line.

alt.src:
Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, b ->        // @JvmStatic + a Consumer parameter
        b.on(ParcelDelivered.class,                          // the Class<E> overload
             d -> delivered.add(Events.grams(d))));           // the facade over Weight; Handler<? super E>
handle.close();                                               // Subscription.close() throws nothing

closing:
We started at a depot with two doors. Now Kotlin callers wire a block with `bus.subscriptions { }`, and Java callers get a facade that still checks everything.

That's Part 3 in one library. The storeroom's labels became `Handler<in E>` and the clerk's note, and the cook's note became `Rejected`. The sign-up sheet became the bus, and the town library's forms and the print shop's units became the model.

Now search your Kotlin code for public `reified` functions: what does a Java caller see?

Next, we'll start Part 4, Inside the JVM, with a theatre company that fetches each prop only when a scene needs it. Java read our Kotlin as class files. Who loads them, and when does their code first run?
recap: A subscription DSL collects what the block declares and subscribes it all at the end: a block that throws subscribes nothing, and one handle closes everything, in reverse order.

`on<E>` is inline and reified. Its lambda is called from inside a `Handler` object, so it must be `crossinline`. A `check` in `on` catches subscriptions made from inside a handler, which `@DslMarker` can't see.
`@DslMarker` on the builder classes makes only the nearest builder implicit, so `timed` inside `timed` stops compiling instead of quietly creating a sibling group.

Java can't call reified functions and stumbles over `KClass`, defaults, objects, companions and value classes. Add `Class<E>` overloads, `@JvmOverloads`, `@JvmStatic`, `@JvmField`, `@file:JvmName`, and a facade that builds the value classes so every check still runs.
In a design review, a choice that an earlier mechanism forces is easy to defend. Write down the judgment calls, and the condition that would make you undo each one.
Where the library stops: it lives in one program's memory, so events that must survive a crash or reach another program need storage of their own, and a slow handler still slows every publish.

quiz.q: From *Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers*: inside `timed("load") { ... }` you call `timed("deliveries") { ... }`. `TimedGroup` has no `timed`; both builder classes carry `@EventsDsl`, which is annotated `@DslMarker`. What happens?
options: It compiles and creates a sibling group under the outer builder
It compiles and nests deliveries inside the load group
It fails to compile: `timed` can't be called with an implicit outer receiver
It compiles, and throws when the block runs
quiz.why: With the marker, only the nearest marked receiver, the `TimedGroup`, is implicit, and it has no `timed`. Without the marker, the first option is exactly what happens, silently, which is why it's tempting. If you do want the sibling, write `this@subscriptions.timed(...)`.

quiz.q: From *Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns*: `inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> on(handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) })` doesn't compile. Which fix fits best?
options: Mark `handler` `crossinline`: it's called from inside the `Handler` object, and its body can still be inlined there
Remove `inline`: the function then works without changes
Mark the function `@PublishedApi`
Change `Handler { handler(it) }` to `handler as Handler<E>`
quiz.why: The lambda runs later, from another object, so a non-local `return` inside it couldn't work, and the compiler asks you to rule it out. `noinline` would compile too, but it keeps a lambda object inside each Handler. Removing `inline` breaks `reified`. The cast doesn't compile either: an inlined lambda parameter can't be used as a value, and even with `noinline` a Kotlin function object is not a `Handler`.

quiz.q: From *Value classes and what they compile to*: Java code writes `new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500L)`, where `ParcelCollected` is a data class with `ParcelId` and `Weight` value-class properties. What happens?
options: It compiles and checks both values
It compiles and skips the `init` blocks
It throws `NoSuchMethodError` when the program runs
javac refuses: `ParcelCollected(String,long) has private access in ParcelCollected`
quiz.why: kotlinc makes that constructor private and adds a public synthetic one with a `DefaultConstructorMarker`, which javac won't call. That's what keeps Java from building an unchecked `ParcelCollected`. The way in is a facade such as `Events.collected(String, long)`, which builds the value classes so their checks run.

quiz.q: From *Type erasure and reified type parameters*: why does the bus keep `subscribe(type: KClass<E>, ...)` and add `subscribe(type: Class<E>, ...)`, rather than offering only the reified `subscribe<E>`?
options: Because reified functions are slower than ones that take a token
Because Java can't call a reified function, so the work must live in a version that takes a class token
Because `KClass` needs kotlin-reflect when the program runs
Because a reified function can't be a member of a class
quiz.why: javac can't inline Kotlin code, so it can't supply `E`, and kotlinc marks the reified function synthetic. The token versions do the work, and the reified one is a one-line wrapper for Kotlin. `KClass` itself needs no kotlin-reflect for `isInstance` and `cast`, and members can be reified.

quiz.q: `class EventBus(middleware: List<Middleware> = emptyList(), onError: ErrorHandler = ErrorHandler.PRINT)`, with no `@JvmOverloads`. Which Java calls compile?
options: Only `new EventBus(list, onError)`
`new EventBus()`, `new EventBus(list)` and `new EventBus(list, onError)`
`new EventBus()` and `new EventBus(list, onError)`, but not `new EventBus(list)`
None: Java can't call constructors with default arguments
quiz.why: When every constructor parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a constructor with no arguments, so Java gets that one and the full one. The ones in between exist only with `@JvmOverloads`, and javac reports `no suitable constructor found` for `new EventBus(list)`. The second option is what the lab's bus offers, because it carries the annotation.

flashcards.front: Why does the subscriptions builder collect first and subscribe at the end?
flashcards.back: A block that throws halfway then subscribes nothing, and the caller gets one handle that closes everything the block declared.

flashcards.front: Why must the lambda of `inline fun <reified E> on(handler: (E) -> Unit)` be `crossinline`?
flashcards.back: The body calls it from inside another object, the `Handler`, which runs later. `crossinline` forbids non-local returns so it can still be inlined there.

flashcards.front: What does `@DslMarker` stop, and what can't it stop?
flashcards.back: It stops implicit calls to an outer marked builder from an inner block. It can't stop a call from inside a handler lambda, which has no receiver: use a runtime check.

flashcards.front: Java can't call your reified `subscribe<E>`. What do you add?
flashcards.back: A `Class<E>` overload that delegates with `type.kotlin`. The reified function stays a one-line wrapper for Kotlin.

flashcards.front: A Kotlin constructor where every parameter has a default: what does Java get without `@JvmOverloads`?
flashcards.back: A constructor with no arguments and the full one. `@JvmOverloads` adds the ones in between.

flashcards.front: Why a facade like `Events.collected(String, long)` instead of `@JvmName` on functions that take value classes?
flashcards.back: The facade builds the value classes, so their `init` checks run. `@JvmName` lets Java pass raw values straight past them.

flashcards.front: What does a Java caller get for free from `Handler<in E>` and a Kotlin sealed model?
flashcards.back: `Handler<? super E>` in every signature, and an exhaustive `switch` over the sealed types with no `default`.

terms.plain: A small language made for one job, written as ordinary Kotlin calls and blocks.
The function that creates a builder, runs your block on it and returns the result, such as `bus.subscriptions { }`.
An annotation for your own DSL marker annotation: inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver can be called implicitly.
A modifier for a lambda parameter of an inline function that is called from another object or lambda; it forbids non-local returns.
A small object of static functions that takes and returns plain Java types and builds the Kotlin types inside.
Makes kotlinc generate one Java overload per trailing default parameter.
Makes a member of an object or companion a real static method, so Java needs no INSTANCE or Companion.
A meeting where you defend each design choice, say what forces it, and say what would make you undo it.

explain_back.prompt: A sceptical reviewer says: "This is a lot of type machinery for an event bus. Why not a `Map<String, MutableList<(Any) -> Unit>>` and a JSON string per event?" Defend your design: name the bugs each choice prevents, and the one or two choices you'd undo.
explain_back.answer: With strings and `Any`, every handler parses and casts for itself: a scan that says "2.5" grams throws inside the load board after the tracking page listed it, a typo in an event name never matches, and a new event type is ignored everywhere without a word. The sealed model and the door stop all three: bad input is rejected once, and a `when` without `else` breaks the build wherever a new type needs handling. Value classes make a swapped id and weight a compile error. The bus walks supertypes, so one tracking handler sees every event, and `Handler<in E>` lets that handler fit any subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. Isolation, handles and a copy-on-write list keep one bad or self-removing handler from hurting the rest. The DSL commits a block all at once, and `@DslMarker` keeps nested blocks from reaching the wrong builder. For Java, the overloads and the facade make it read like a Java library without skipping a check. What I'd undo: the unbounded `DropDuplicates`, which should become a bounded window or a record kept by the handler. And anything that must survive a crash goes to storage that outlives the program, not to this bus.

deeper.body:
A production version of this library would add, roughly in this order:

- Asynchronous lanes. An executor per group of handlers, with one single-threaded lane per tracking number so the events for one parcel keep their order, and a bounded queue in front of each lane. That's also where backpressure lives, the idea of a slow receiver slowing a fast sender: when a lane is full, the publisher waits, or the event is kept to try again later.
- Real metrics. Replace `Timings` with timers from a metrics library such as Micrometer, named after each subscription, so a slow handler shows up on the same dashboards as the rest of the program.
- Durability. Events that must survive a crash, or reach other programs, go into a database table in the same transaction as the change that caused them (a pattern often called an outbox), and a separate job sends them on to a message broker. The in-process bus stays for connecting the parts of one program.
- A shelf for refused scans. `Parsed.Rejected` goes to a store with its reason, a counter, and a small tool to replay the scans once the bug behind them is fixed.
- Versioned events. Stable type names with `@SerialName` if you serialize with kotlinx.serialization, and parser branches that map old names to new types.
- A checked public API. `on<E>` and `subscribe<E>` are public inline functions, so their bodies are compiled into every caller, and the `@JvmOverloads` overloads are part of what Java callers link against. A binary-compatibility check in the build catches a change that would break callers compiled against the previous version.
- `@JvmExposeBoxed`, once it is stable, if it also covers interface members. Until then, the `Events` facade is the Java door.

One thing it should not add is registration by scanning for annotations, Guava style (`@Subscribe` on methods, found through reflection). Guava's own documentation lists the costs: subscribers are hard to find from the publisher, and reflection breaks under the tools that shrink and rename code for release. Explicit `on<E>` calls keep every subscription visible in the code that owns it.
